q: A machine costing Rs 6,60,000 generates a net cash inflow of Rs 1,10,000 per year. Its payback period is:

options.A: 5 years
options.B: 4 years
options.C: 6 years
options.D: 6.6 years

e: With uniform annual inflows, payback = initial cost / annual cash inflow = 6,60,000 / 1,10,000 = 6 years.

q: A project costing Rs 5,00,000 yields net cash inflows of Rs 1,00,000 in Year 1, Rs 1,50,000 in Year 2 and Rs 3,00,000 in Year 3. Its payback period is:

options.A: 2 years 10 months
options.B: 2 years 6 months
options.C: 3 years
options.D: 2 years 4 months

e: Cumulative inflows: Year 1 Rs 1,00,000, Year 2 Rs 2,50,000. The balance Rs 2,50,000 comes from Year 3's Rs 3,00,000 in 2,50,000/3,00,000 x 12 = 10 months. Payback = 2 years 10 months.

q: A project involves an initial investment of Rs 5,00,000 with no salvage value, so that the average investment over its life is Rs 2,50,000. If the average annual profit after depreciation and tax is Rs 50,000, the Average Rate of Return computed on the average investment is:
e: ARR on average investment = average annual profit / average investment x 100 = 50,000 / 2,50,000 x 100 = 20%.

q: A project's internal rate of return is 12%, while the enterprise's cost of capital is 14%. The correct decision is to:

options.A: Accept the project, since its IRR is positive
options.B: Reject the project, since at a 14% discount rate its NPV would be negative
options.C: Accept the project, since the IRR exceeds the bank rate
options.D: Postpone the decision until the payback period is computed

e: A project is acceptable only if its IRR exceeds the cost of capital, the minimum required return. Here 12% is below 14%, so discounting at 14% gives a negative NPV and the project is rejected.

q: If the NPV and IRR methods give conflicting rankings of two mutually exclusive projects, the project to be selected is the one with the:

options.A: Higher IRR, in all cases
options.B: Shorter payback period
options.C: Higher NPV, because NPV measures the addition to wealth discounted at the cost of capital
options.D: Higher average rate of return

e: NPV and IRR can conflict because of differing reinvestment assumptions and project scale. NPV, measured at the cost of capital, directly shows the addition to the firm's wealth, so it prevails.

q: Multiple (more than one) internal rates of return for a project can arise when:

options.A: The project has a very long life
options.B: The initial outlay is very large
options.C: The discount rate changes every year
options.D: The project's cash flows are non-conventional, i.e., they change sign more than once over its life

e: Each sign change in the cash-flow stream can produce another IRR. Projects with outflows interspersed with inflows (non-conventional flows) can therefore yield multiple internal rates of return.

q: For the purpose of capital budgeting, the cash flows relevant to a project are:

options.A: The incremental cash flows, after tax, that arise only if the project is undertaken
options.B: The total accounting profits of the enterprise after the project is taken up
options.C: The gross cash inflows of the project before tax
options.D: All cash flows of the enterprise, whether or not connected with the project

e: Capital budgeting considers only the additional, after-tax cash flows caused by the project itself. Sunk costs and non-incremental overheads are irrelevant; opportunity costs of resources used are relevant.

q: In DCF appraisal of a project, the additional working capital required to support the project is treated as:

options.A: Ignored altogether, since it is not a capital cost
options.B: A cash outflow at the commencement of the project and a cash inflow (recovery) at the end of its life
options.C: A revenue expense of the first year only
options.D: A permanent addition to the capital cost of the project, which is never recovered

e: Working capital invested in a project is a cash outflow when committed but is recovered when the project ends, so it is also shown as a cash inflow in the final year of appraisal.

q: A company's capital structure consists of equity capital of Rs 5,00,000 (cost 14%), preference capital of Rs 1,00,000 (cost 10%) and debt of Rs 4,00,000 (after-tax cost 8%). Its weighted average cost of capital is:

A share is expected to pay a dividend of Rs 6 per share next year. Its market price is Rs 50 and dividends are expected to grow at a constant rate of 5% per year. Using the dividend growth model, the cost of equity is:
e: Cost of equity = (expected dividend / market price) + growth rate = (6 / 50) + 5% = 12% + 5% = 17%.

q: A company issues 10% preference shares of face value Rs 100 each at Rs 95 per share. The cost of preference capital is:
e: Cost of irredeemable preference capital = annual dividend / net proceeds per share = 10 / 95 x 100 = 10.53%, the discount on issue raising the effective cost.

q: Using the Capital Asset Pricing Model, where the risk-free rate is 7%, the expected market return is 13% and the beta of the share is 1.2, the cost of equity is:
e: CAPM: cost of equity = risk-free rate + beta x (market return - risk-free rate) = 7% + 1.2 x (13% - 7%) = 7% + 7.2% = 14.2%.

q: The 'marginal cost of capital' means:

options.A: The average cost of all the capital raised in the past
options.B: The cost of the cheapest source of finance available
options.C: The cost of raising an additional rupee of capital by the enterprise
options.D: The interest paid on the last debenture issue only

e: Marginal cost of capital is the weighted average cost of the new, additional funds raised, as distinct from the historical average cost of funds already in use.

q: In computing the weighted average cost of capital, the weights assigned to the different sources of finance should preferably be based on:

options.A: Book values as shown in the balance sheet
options.B: Face values of the securities issued
options.C: The amounts sanctioned by the Board of Directors
options.D: Market values of the securities

e: Market-value weights reflect the current economic importance of each source and the target structure investors actually price, so they are preferred over book or face values for WACC.

q: An enterprise has a profit before interest and tax of Rs 4,00,000 and pays interest of Rs 1,00,000. Its degree of financial leverage is:
e: Degree of financial leverage = PBIT / (PBIT - interest) = 4,00,000 / (4,00,000 - 1,00,000) = 4,00,000 / 3,00,000 = 1.33.

q: An enterprise has sales of Rs 10,00,000, variable costs of Rs 4,00,000, fixed costs of Rs 3,00,000 and interest of Rs 1,00,000. Its degree of combined leverage is:
e: Contribution = 10,00,000 - 4,00,000 = Rs 6,00,000; profit before tax = 6,00,000 - 3,00,000 - 1,00,000 = Rs 2,00,000. Combined leverage = contribution / PBT = 6,00,000 / 2,00,000 = 3.0.

q: Trading on equity (the use of debt in the capital structure) benefits the equity shareholders only when:

options.A: The rate of interest on debt is the lowest in the market
options.B: The enterprise has no preference capital
options.C: The return on investment earned by the enterprise exceeds the rate of interest payable on the borrowed funds
options.D: The debt-equity ratio is exactly 1 : 1

e: Trading on equity works only when the funds borrowed earn a return higher than the fixed interest payable; the surplus then accrues to equity shareholders and raises their return.

q: 'Financial risk' of an enterprise refers to:

options.A: The risk of a fall in sales due to competition
options.B: The risk of physical damage to its assets
options.C: The risk arising from changes in technology
options.D: The risk arising from the use of fixed-charge sources of finance (debt), i.e., variability in the earnings of equity holders and the possible inability to meet fixed financial charges

e: Financial risk is the extra risk borne by equity holders because fixed interest and preference charges must be met from variable earnings, magnifying the variability of their returns and the danger of default.

q: The optimum capital structure of an enterprise is the combination of debt and equity which:

options.A: Minimises the overall (weighted average) cost of capital and thereby maximises the value of the enterprise
options.B: Contains no debt at all
options.C: Maximises the proportion of debt
options.D: Keeps the current ratio at 2 : 1

e: The optimum capital structure is that mix of debt and equity at which the weighted average cost of capital is lowest; at that point the market value of the enterprise is highest.

q: An enterprise is said to be 'highly geared' when:

options.A: Its equity capital is much larger than its fixed assets
options.B: The proportion of fixed-cost-bearing capital (preference capital and debt) is high in relation to equity shareholders' funds
options.C: It has a very large number of shareholders
options.D: Its shares are listed and actively traded on a stock exchange

e: A highly geared company has a large proportion of fixed-charge capital (debentures, loans, preference shares) relative to equity, so a small change in profits causes a large change in equity earnings.

q: Sales of an enterprise are Rs 8,00,000 and the cost of goods sold is Rs 5,60,000. Its gross profit ratio is:
Current assets of an enterprise are Rs 5,00,000, comprising stock of Rs 2,00,000 and prepaid expenses of Rs 50,000. Current liabilities are Rs 2,50,000. The quick (acid-test) ratio is:
e: Quick assets = current assets - stock - prepaid expenses = 5,00,000 - 2,00,000 - 50,000 = Rs 2,50,000. Quick ratio = 2,50,000 / 2,50,000 = 1 : 1.

q: Credit sales of an enterprise are Rs 7,30,000 and its average debtors are Rs 1,00,000. The average collection period is:

options.A: 50 days
options.B: 73 days
options.C: 36.5 days
options.D: 45 days

e: Average collection period = average debtors / credit sales x 365 = 1,00,000 / 7,30,000 x 365 = 50 days.

q: Credit purchases of an enterprise are Rs 3,65,000 and its average creditors are Rs 50,000. The average payment period is:

options.A: 25 days
options.B: 50 days
options.C: 73 days
options.D: 40 days

e: Average payment period = average creditors / credit purchases x 365 = 50,000 / 3,65,000 x 365 = 50 days.

q: Proprietors' funds of an enterprise are Rs 6,00,000 and its total assets are Rs 10,00,000. The proprietary ratio is:
e: Proprietary ratio = proprietors' funds / total assets = 6,00,000 / 10,00,000 = 0.6 : 1, showing owners finance 60% of the total assets.

q: Net sales of an enterprise are Rs 15,00,000 and its total assets are Rs 5,00,000. Its total assets turnover ratio is:

options.A: 0.33 times
options.B: 1.5 times
options.C: 2 times
options.D: 3 times

e: Total assets turnover = net sales / total assets = 15,00,000 / 5,00,000 = 3 times.

q: Net sales of an enterprise are Rs 10,00,000 and its working capital is Rs 2,00,000. The working capital turnover ratio is:

options.A: 5 times
options.B: 0.2 times
options.C: 2 times
options.D: 10 times

e: Working capital turnover = net sales / working capital = 10,00,000 / 2,00,000 = 5 times.

q: A company's Earnings Per Share is Rs 10 and its Dividend Per Share is Rs 4. Its dividend payout ratio is:
e: Dividend payout ratio = dividend per share / earnings per share x 100 = 4 / 10 x 100 = 40%; the balance 60% is retained.

q: The market price of a company's share is Rs 120 and its Earnings Per Share is Rs 10. The price-earnings (P/E) ratio is:
e: P/E ratio = market price per share / earnings per share = 120 / 10 = 12, i.e. investors pay twelve times current earnings.

q: In computing Return on Capital Employed, profit before interest and tax (PBIT) is used as the numerator, rather than profit after interest, because:

options.A: Interest is not an expense of the enterprise
options.B: Tax rates differ from one enterprise to another
options.C: PBIT is always larger than the net profit
options.D: The denominator (capital employed) includes funds provided by long-term lenders as well as by owners, so the return must be measured before paying the lenders their interest

e: Capital employed includes long-term debt as well as owners' funds. PBIT is the return earned for all these providers before interest is paid out, so it matches the denominator.

q: The net profit of an enterprise is Rs 1,00,000, after charging depreciation of Rs 30,000 and after crediting a profit of Rs 10,000 on the sale of machinery. The funds from operations are:
e: Funds from operations = net profit + depreciation (non-fund item) - profit on sale of machinery (non-operating, shown separately as a source) = 1,00,000 + 30,000 - 10,000 = Rs 1,20,000.

q: Which of the following is NOT a source of funds?

options.A: Issue of shares for cash
options.B: Depreciation charged in the profit and loss account
options.C: Long-term loan raised from a bank
options.D: Sale of fixed assets

e: Depreciation is a non-cash charge added back to profit in computing funds from operations; it is not itself a source of funds. Funds come from operations, share issues, loans and asset sales.

q: Which of the following transactions involves no flow of funds?

options.A: Issue of shares for cash
options.B: Sale of investments
options.C: Conversion of debentures into equity shares
options.D: Raising of a long-term loan

e: A fund flow arises only when a transaction changes working capital through a current and a non-current account. Converting debentures into shares affects two non-current accounts, so there is no flow of funds.

q: Under Accounting Standard 3 (AS-3), for a non-financial enterprise, interest paid is classified in the cash flow statement as a:

options.A: Operating activity
options.B: Investing activity
options.C: Non-cash activity, not shown in the statement at all
options.D: Financing activity

e: Under AS-3, for non-financial enterprises interest paid is a financing activity (cost of obtaining finance), while for financial enterprises it is an operating activity.

q: In the schedule of changes in working capital, an increase in stock (a current asset) during the year results in:

options.A: An increase in working capital
options.B: A decrease in working capital
options.C: No change in working capital
options.D: An increase in funds from operations

e: Working capital is current assets minus current liabilities. An increase in a current asset like stock, other things equal, raises the excess of current assets and hence working capital.

q: In computing the Economic Internal Rate of Return (EIRR) of a railway project, the project inputs and outputs are generally valued at 'shadow prices', which represent:

options.A: The prices fixed by the Railway Board for departmental purposes
options.B: The true economic (opportunity) cost or value to society, as distinct from possibly distorted market prices
options.C: The historical cost of the assets involved
options.D: The prices prevailing in foreign markets

e: Shadow prices adjust market prices for distortions like taxes, subsidies and controls to reflect the real opportunity cost or benefit to the economy, and are used in the economic (as against financial) appraisal.

q: The losses borne by Indian Railways on account of services rendered at below-cost rates - such as concessional travel and the operation of uneconomic branch lines - are described as:

options.A: Operating losses of the Railways
options.B: Hidden reserves of the Railways
options.C: Social service obligations (social burden) on the Railways
options.D: Sunk costs of the Railways

e: Social service obligations are the quantified losses Railways bear in discharging social responsibilities - concessional fares, uneconomic lines, etc. - which a purely commercial undertaking would avoid.

q: The dividend payable by Indian Railways on its capital-at-charge (capital invested out of general revenues) is paid to:

options.A: The Railway Safety Fund
options.B: The Development Fund
options.C: IRFC
options.D: General Revenues

e: Dividend on capital-at-charge is the return payable by Railways to the Government on capital invested from general revenues, and is credited to General Revenues after the budget merger arrangements.

q: In the financial appraisal of a new railway line, a sensitivity test would typically involve recomputing the anticipated rate of return on the assumption that:

options.A: Projected traffic earnings fall short of, or working expenses exceed, the estimates by a stated margin
options.B: The project is completed exactly on the scheduled date
options.C: The capital cost remains unchanged
options.D: The dividend rate on capital-at-charge is increased

e: Sensitivity analysis tests the robustness of a project by recomputing its return under adverse variations - typically a shortfall in earnings or an excess in working expenses - to see if it still clears the test rate.

q: A railway work whose anticipated rate of return works out to less than the prescribed 10% test of remunerativeness is classified as:

options.A: Remunerative
options.B: Unremunerative
options.C: Self-liquidating
options.D: A safety work

e: Indian Railways prescribe a 10% rate of return (financial justification test) for remunerative works. A work falling short of 10% is unremunerative and needs special justification, e.g. on safety or strategic grounds.

q: Budgeted sales of a product are 50,000 units. The opening stock is 5,000 units and the closing stock is to be 8,000 units. The production budget should provide for production of:

options.A: 47,000 units
options.B: 53,000 units
options.C: 45,000 units
options.D: 63,000 units

e: Production = budgeted sales + closing stock - opening stock = 50,000 + 8,000 - 5,000 = 53,000 units.

q: Production of 20,000 units is budgeted, each unit requiring 2 kg of material. The opening stock of material is 4,000 kg and the closing stock is to be 6,000 kg. The quantity of material to be purchased is:
e: Material usage = 20,000 units x 2 kg = 40,000 kg. Purchases = usage + closing stock - opening stock = 40,000 + 6,000 - 4,000 = 42,000 kg.

q: A cash budget shows an opening cash balance of Rs 40,000, estimated receipts of Rs 2,60,000 and estimated payments of Rs 2,85,000 for a month. The closing cash balance will be:
e: Closing cash balance = opening balance + receipts - payments = 40,000 + 2,60,000 - 2,85,000 = Rs 15,000.

q: The principal purpose of preparing a cash budget is to:

options.A: Determine the profit of the enterprise for the period
options.B: Value the closing inventory of finished goods
options.C: Forecast cash receipts and payments period by period, so that borrowing can be arranged for shortages and surplus cash invested in advance
options.D: Fix the selling prices of the products

e: A cash budget is a period-wise forecast of receipts and payments; knowing likely shortages and surpluses in advance lets management arrange borrowings and deploy idle cash profitably.

q: A budget manual is:

options.A: A document which sets out the responsibilities of the executives involved and the procedures, instructions and forms to be followed in preparing budgets
options.B: The register in which actual expenditure is recorded
options.C: Another name for the master budget
options.D: A manual of accounting standards issued for statutory audit

e: The budget manual documents the whole budgetary system - who prepares which budget, the timetable, procedures, forms and lines of authority - so that budgeting is done uniformly.

q: The main function of a budget committee is to:

options.A: Prepare the annual accounts of the enterprise
options.B: Coordinate the preparation of the functional budgets, resolve differences between departments and approve the budgets
options.C: Conduct the internal audit of the enterprise
options.D: Fix the wages and salaries of the staff

e: The budget committee, usually headed by a senior executive, coordinates and reconciles the functional budgets prepared by departments, settles conflicts and approves the final master budget.

q: A fixed budget loses much of its usefulness for control purposes when:

options.A: Costs are predominantly variable in nature
options.B: The budget period is a full year
options.C: Prices of materials remain stable
options.D: The actual level of activity differs considerably from the level for which the budget was prepared

e: A fixed budget is drawn for one planned activity level. If actual activity differs greatly, its cost figures are not comparable with actuals, so it fails as a control tool - a flexible budget is needed.

q: A budget provides for fixed costs of Rs 1,50,000 and variable costs of Rs 12 per unit at an activity level of 15,000 units. The total flexed budget allowance at an actual output of 12,000 units is:
e: Flexed allowance = fixed costs + variable cost at actual output = 1,50,000 + (12 x 12,000) = 1,50,000 + 1,44,000 = Rs 2,94,000. Fixed costs are not scaled with output.

q: The capital expenditure budget of an enterprise primarily deals with:

options.A: The planned outlay on acquisition of long-term assets such as plant, machinery and buildings
options.B: Day-to-day revenue expenses of running the business
options.C: Payment of wages and salaries to staff
options.D: Collection of dues from debtors

e: The capital expenditure budget plans investment in long-term assets - plant, machinery, buildings and other works - whose benefits extend over several years, with proper authorisation and financing.

q: Budgetary slack arises when managers, while preparing budgets:

options.A: Exceed their budgeted expenditure during the year
options.B: Deliberately under-estimate revenues or over-estimate costs, so that the targets become easier to achieve
options.C: Refuse to prepare budgets for their departments
options.D: Transfer funds from one budget head to another

e: Budgetary slack is the deliberate cushion built into budgets by understating expected revenue or overstating expected costs, making targets easy to beat but reducing the budget's planning value.

q: Which of the following is NOT a functional budget?

options.A: Sales budget
options.B: Production budget
options.C: Materials budget
options.D: Budgeted balance sheet

e: Functional budgets cover operating functions - sales, production, materials, labour, cash and so on. The budgeted balance sheet is a part of the master budget, not a functional budget.

q: A major practical difficulty in implementing zero-base budgeting is that:

options.A: It requires no justification of any expenditure
options.B: It can be applied only to capital works
options.C: It is highly time-consuming, and ranking a large number of decision packages — especially of support and service activities whose output is hard to measure — is difficult
options.D: It cannot be used by government departments at all

e: Zero-base budgeting requires every activity to be justified from scratch through decision packages. Preparing and ranking many packages, especially for support services with unmeasurable output, is very time-consuming.

q: Under zero-base budgeting, if a decision package is not approved even at its minimum (survival) level of funding, it implies that:

options.A: The activity should be discontinued altogether
options.B: The activity automatically continues at last year's level
options.C: The activity is transferred to another department
options.D: The package is approved automatically in the next year

e: Under ZBB each package has a minimum survival level below which the activity cannot function at all. If even that level is not funded, the activity has no justification and is dropped.

q: The Outcome Budget, introduced by the Government of India in 2005-06, primarily seeks to:

options.A: Replace the Demands for Grants altogether
options.B: Increase the total size of the budget
options.C: Present only the financial outlays of the ministries
options.D: Convert financial outlays into measurable outcomes, linking the expenditure of ministries to the results achieved

e: The Outcome Budget translates budgeted outlays into physical outcomes and results to be achieved, so Parliament and the public can judge what public money actually buys.

q: The estimated annual operating cost of an enterprise is Rs 24,00,000 (reckoning a year of 360 days). Its operating cycle is 60 days. On the operating-cycle method, the working capital required is:
e: Working capital = annual operating cost x operating cycle / 360 = 24,00,000 x 60 / 360 = Rs 4,00,000.

q: In a manufacturing concern, raw materials are stored for 30 days, the production process takes 15 days, finished goods are stored for 20 days and debtors are collected in 40 days. Creditors allow 25 days' credit. The length of the operating (cash conversion) cycle is:

options.A: 65 days
options.B: 105 days
options.C: 80 days
options.D: 90 days

e: Operating cycle = raw material storage 30 + production 15 + finished goods storage 20 + debtors collection 40 - creditors credit 25 = 80 days.

q: Under the matching (hedging) approach to financing working capital:

options.A: Permanent working capital and fixed assets are financed from long-term sources, while temporary (seasonal) working capital is financed from short-term sources
options.B: The entire working capital is financed from short-term borrowings
options.C: All assets of the enterprise are financed from equity alone
options.D: Temporary working capital is financed from long-term loans

e: The matching or hedging approach matches the maturity of finance with the life of the asset: permanent needs from long-term sources and short seasonal needs from short-term sources, balancing cost and risk.

q: An aggressive working capital financing policy is one in which:

options.A: Long-term funds are used even for meeting seasonal needs
options.B: No short-term borrowing is resorted to at all
options.C: Current assets are maintained at very high levels
options.D: Even a part of the permanent working capital is financed by short-term funds, which lowers cost but increases risk

e: An aggressive policy finances even part of permanent working capital with cheaper short-term funds. It lowers the cost of finance but raises the risk of non-renewal and liquidity trouble.

q: Over-trading means:

options.A: Carrying on all trade strictly on a cash basis
options.B: Expanding business operations rapidly without adequate working capital to support them, resulting in liquidity strain
options.C: Selling goods at prices above the prevailing market rate
options.D: Deliberately maintaining excessive inventory of all items

e: Over-trading is doing business beyond the capacity of the working capital available - rapid sales growth with rising debtors and creditors but insufficient liquid funds, leading to a liquidity crisis despite profits.

q: Negative working capital in an enterprise indicates that:

options.A: Current assets exceed current liabilities
options.B: The enterprise carries no working capital at all
options.C: Current liabilities exceed current assets
options.D: The fixed assets of the enterprise have a negative value

e: Working capital = current assets - current liabilities. It is negative when current liabilities exceed current assets, meaning short-term obligations are partly financing long-term assets.

q: Compared with a trading concern, a manufacturing concern generally requires more working capital mainly because:

options.A: Its operating cycle is longer, with funds locked up successively in raw materials, work-in-progress and finished goods
options.B: It sells its products only for cash
options.C: It never has any debtors
options.D: Its fixed costs are lower than those of a trading concern

e: A manufacturing concern's funds pass through raw materials, work-in-progress and finished goods before sale, making its operating cycle longer than a trading concern's and its working capital needs larger.

q: A liberalisation of credit standards (granting credit more freely to customers) generally results in:

options.A: A decrease in the sales volume of the enterprise
options.B: A decrease in bad debts
options.C: An immediate improvement in the liquidity of the enterprise
options.D: An increase in sales, but also higher bad debts, higher collection costs and more funds blocked in receivables

e: Easier credit standards raise sales, but part of the increase comes from weaker customers, so bad debts, collection effort and investment in receivables all go up.

q: The annual credit sales of an enterprise are Rs 12,00,000 and its average debtors are Rs 2,00,000. Taking a year of 360 days, the average collection period is:

options.A: 30 days
options.B: 60 days
options.C: 45 days
options.D: 90 days

e: Average collection period = average debtors / credit sales x 360 = 2,00,000 / 12,00,000 x 360 = 60 days.

q: A supplier offers credit terms of 2/10, net 30. The approximate annual cost of not taking the cash discount (on a 360-day year basis) is:
e: Cost of forgoing the discount = (2/98) x (360 / (30 - 10)) = 2.04% x 18 = 36.7% per annum, the price of using the supplier's money for 20 extra days.

q: The maximum consumption of a material is 400 units per week and the maximum delivery period is 6 weeks. The re-order level for the material is:

options.A: 2,400 units
options.B: 2,000 units
options.C: 1,600 units
options.D: 4,000 units

e: Re-order level = maximum consumption x maximum delivery period = 400 units x 6 weeks = 2,400 units.

q: The re-order level of a material is 3,000 units and the re-order quantity is 2,000 units. Minimum consumption is 250 units per week and the minimum delivery period is 4 weeks. The maximum stock level is:

options.A: 5,000 units
options.B: 6,000 units
options.C: 3,500 units
options.D: 4,000 units

e: Maximum stock level = re-order level + re-order quantity - (minimum consumption x minimum delivery period) = 3,000 + 2,000 - (250 x 4) = 4,000 units.

q: Safety (buffer) stock is maintained primarily to:

options.A: Earn quantity discounts on bulk purchases
options.B: Protect against fluctuations in usage and delivery time and thereby avoid stock-outs
options.C: Increase the value of the closing inventory
options.D: Reduce the re-order quantity of the material

e: Safety stock is the cushion held against uncertainty - unexpected surges in usage or late deliveries - so that production and services are not interrupted by stock-outs.

q: In VED analysis, stores items are classified as Vital, Essential and Desirable on the basis of:

options.A: Their annual consumption value
options.B: Their unit price
options.C: The criticality of the item, that is, the seriousness of the consequences of its non-availability for production or services
options.D: Their physical size and weight

e: VED analysis classifies items by criticality: Vital items whose absence stops production or services, Essential items whose absence causes serious difficulty, and Desirable items that can be missed briefly.

q: The Just-in-Time (JIT) system of inventory management aims at:

options.A: Receiving materials just in time for use in production, so that inventory holding is reduced to the minimum
options.B: Holding the maximum possible inventory at all times
options.C: Purchasing the whole year's requirement in a single bulk order
options.D: Maintaining very large safety stocks of every item

e: JIT seeks near-zero inventory by having suppliers deliver small quantities exactly when production needs them, cutting holding costs, though it demands reliable suppliers and stable schedules.

q: Under the Baumol model of cash management, an enterprise's annual cash requirement is Rs 8,00,000, the cost of converting marketable securities into cash is Rs 25 per transaction and the opportunity interest rate is 10% per annum. The optimum cash balance, sqrt(2AT/i), is:
e: Optimum cash balance = sqrt(2 x 8,00,000 x 25 / 0.10) = sqrt(4,00,000,000) = Rs 20,000, balancing conversion cost against interest foregone.

q: The Miller-Orr model of cash management is designed for enterprises whose cash balances:

options.A: Remain constant throughout the year
options.B: Fluctuate randomly from day to day; the model sets control limits — surplus cash is invested when the balance touches the upper limit and investments are sold when it touches the lower limit
options.C: Are always in deficit
options.D: Are determined entirely by the bank

e: The Miller-Orr model suits random cash flows: balances are allowed to wander between set lower and upper control limits, investing surplus or selling investments only when a limit is hit.

q: According to Keynes, the motives for holding cash are:

options.A: Transaction motive only
options.B: Transaction and investment motives
options.C: Transaction, precautionary and speculative motives
options.D: Precautionary and dividend motives

e: Keynes identified three motives for holding cash: the transaction motive for day-to-day payments, the precautionary motive for contingencies, and the speculative motive for taking advantage of opportunities.

q: Under the lock-box system of accelerating cash collections:

options.A: Customers mail their cheques to a post-office box located near them, which the enterprise's bank empties and credits promptly, reducing postal and processing float
options.B: All cash collections are kept locked in the office safe
options.C: Defaulting debtors are locked out of further credit
options.D: Payments to creditors are deliberately delayed

e: In a lock-box system, customers post cheques to a local post-office box; the bank collects and credits them the same day, cutting mail, processing and clearing float and speeding up realisation.

q: A division earns a profit of Rs 3,00,000 on capital employed of Rs 20,00,000. The cost of capital is 12%. The Residual Income of the division is:
e: Residual income = profit - (capital employed x cost of capital) = 3,00,000 - (20,00,000 x 12%) = 3,00,000 - 2,40,000 = Rs 60,000.

q: Residual Income is considered superior to Return on Investment as a measure of divisional performance because it:

options.A: Is much easier to compute than ROI
options.B: Encourages divisions to accept every project earning more than the cost of capital, whereas ROI may lead a division to reject a project earning above the cost of capital but below its present ROI
options.C: Ignores the cost of capital altogether
options.D: Always gives a higher figure than ROI

e: RI measures absolute surplus over the cost of capital, so any project earning above that cost raises RI. Under ROI, a division may reject such a project if it dilutes its existing percentage return.

q: The Balanced Scorecard evaluates the performance of an organisation from the following four perspectives:

options.A: Sales, production, finance and personnel
options.B: Cost, quality, time and output
options.C: Financial, customer, internal business processes, and learning and growth
options.D: Planning, organising, directing and controlling

e: The Balanced Scorecard views performance through four linked perspectives: financial, customer, internal business processes, and learning and growth, combining financial results with their non-financial drivers.

q: A revenue centre is a responsibility centre whose manager is accountable for:

options.A: The revenues generated by the centre, as in a sales office, without responsibility for the cost of the products sold
options.B: Only the costs incurred by the centre
options.C: The profit earned by the centre
options.D: The capital invested in the centre

e: A revenue centre's manager is answerable only for revenues earned, e.g. a sales office or a railway's commercial earnings unit; the cost of what is sold is not his responsibility.

q: Management audit refers to:

options.A: The audit of the financial statements of an enterprise
options.B: The audit of government accounts conducted by the C&AG
options.C: The checking of vouchers by the internal auditor
options.D: A systematic and independent appraisal of the overall performance and efficiency of management in achieving the objectives of the organisation

e: Management audit is an independent, constructive appraisal of how well management at all levels plans, organises and controls to achieve objectives - broader than financial or internal audit.

q: Under the Current Purchasing Power (CPP) method of inflation accounting:

options.A: Assets are restated at their current replacement cost
options.B: Historical cost accounts are restated in units of current purchasing power with the help of a general price index
options.C: Only monetary items are recorded in the accounts
options.D: The effects of inflation are ignored in the accounts

e: Under CPP, historical figures are restated into rupees of equal current purchasing power using a general price-level index, so comparisons and capital maintenance are in uniform units.

q: Under the Lev and Schwartz model of human resource accounting, the value of the human resources of an organisation is estimated as:

options.A: The total salary paid to the employees since their appointment
options.B: The cost of replacing all the employees
options.C: The present value of the future earnings of the employees up to their retirement
options.D: The training cost incurred on the employees

e: The Lev and Schwartz model values human resources at the present value of employees' expected future earnings (salaries) up to retirement, discounted at an appropriate rate.

q: Value engineering (value analysis) is a technique which aims at:

options.A: Increasing the selling price of the product
options.B: Reducing the quality specifications of the product
options.C: Adding the maximum possible features to the product
options.D: Achieving the essential functions of a product at the lowest total cost, without sacrificing quality, reliability or performance

e: Value engineering systematically examines every function of a product to eliminate unnecessary cost while fully preserving required function, quality, reliability and performance.

q: In target costing, the target cost of a product is determined as:

options.A: The expected market (selling) price minus the desired profit margin
options.B: The actual cost of the previous model, adjusted for inflation
options.C: The actual cost plus a fixed percentage mark-up
options.D: The lowest cost reported by any competitor

e: Target costing starts from the price the market will bear and deducts the profit the firm must earn; the remainder is the allowable (target) cost that design and production must achieve.

q: Kaizen costing is concerned with:

options.A: Determining the cost of a product before production begins
options.B: Continuous and gradual reduction of costs during the manufacturing stage, through small improvements in processes and activities
options.C: The costing of services rendered to customers
options.D: Fixing the target selling price of a product

e: Kaizen costing pursues small, continuous cost reductions during actual production - through steady process improvements by the workforce - unlike target costing, which works at the design stage.

q: Life-cycle costing takes into account:

options.A: Only the manufacturing cost of a product
options.B: Only the research and development cost of a product
options.C: All costs over the entire life of a product — from design and development, through production and use, to withdrawal and disposal
options.D: The costs of one accounting year only

e: Life-cycle costing accumulates all costs of a product over its whole life - development, introduction, growth, maturity, decline and disposal - revealing its true total cost and profitability.

q: In throughput accounting, based on the Theory of Constraints, 'throughput' is defined as:

options.A: Sales revenue minus all operating expenses of the factory
options.B: The gross profit earned by the factory
options.C: The contribution earned per machine hour
options.D: Sales revenue minus the totally variable costs (essentially the direct material cost), the object being to maximise throughput at the bottleneck resource

e: Throughput in the Theory of Constraints is sales minus totally variable cost (essentially direct materials). Maximising throughput per unit of the bottleneck resource improves the whole system's performance.

q: Conversion cost of a product is the cost of converting raw material into the finished product and comprises:

options.A: Direct material and direct labour
options.B: Direct labour and factory (manufacturing) overheads
options.C: Total cost less selling overheads
options.D: Prime cost and administration overheads

e: Conversion cost is the cost of converting material into finished goods - direct labour plus factory (manufacturing) overheads. Direct material is excluded because it is the thing being converted.

q: An out-of-pocket cost is a cost which:

options.A: Has already been incurred in the past and cannot be recovered
options.B: Is a notional cost involving no cash payment, such as interest on own capital
options.C: Remains fixed in total at all levels of activity
options.D: Involves an actual cash payment, e.g., wages, materials and power, as distinct from non-cash costs like depreciation

e: An out-of-pocket cost requires an actual cash outlay, e.g. wages, materials and power. It contrasts with book costs like depreciation and notional costs like interest on own capital.

q: Committed fixed costs are those which:

options.A: Arise from past decisions and the possession of plant and facilities — e.g., depreciation, rent under a lease and insurance — and cannot be materially reduced in the short run
options.B: Can be increased or decreased at the discretion of management each year, like research and publicity expenditure
options.C: Vary in direct proportion to the level of output
options.D: Are incurred only when production exceeds the normal capacity

e: Committed fixed costs result from earlier decisions to acquire plant and facilities - depreciation, lease rent, insurance - and are largely unavoidable in the short run even if output falls.

q: Works (factory) cost of production is computed as:

options.A: Prime cost plus administration overheads
options.B: Cost of goods sold plus selling overheads
options.C: Prime cost plus factory overheads, adjusted for opening and closing work-in-progress
options.D: Direct material plus direct labour only

e: Works cost = prime cost + factory overheads, adjusted for the net change in work-in-progress (opening WIP added, closing WIP deducted), representing cost up to the factory gate.

q: The total cost of producing 5,000 units is Rs 38,000 and that of producing 9,000 units is Rs 54,000. Using the high-low method, the variable cost per unit is:

options.A: Rs 2
options.B: Rs 4
options.C: Rs 5
options.D: Rs 8

e: Variable cost per unit = (54,000 - 38,000) / (9,000 - 5,000) = 16,000 / 4,000 = Rs 4 per unit by the high-low method.

q: The re-order level of a material is 4,800 units. Normal consumption is 400 units per week and the normal delivery period is 5 weeks. The minimum stock level is:

options.A: 2,000 units
options.B: 3,200 units
options.C: 2,800 units
options.D: 4,800 units

e: Minimum stock level = re-order level - (normal consumption x normal delivery period) = 4,800 - (400 x 5) = 4,800 - 2,000 = 2,800 units.

q: The annual consumption of a material is 2,500 units. The cost of placing an order is Rs 32 and the carrying cost is Rs 4 per unit per year. Using EOQ = sqrt(2AO/C), the Economic Order Quantity is:

options.A: 200 units
options.B: 250 units
options.C: 400 units
options.D: 100 units

e: EOQ = sqrt(2 x 2,500 x 32 / 4) = sqrt(40,000) = 200 units, the order size that minimises total ordering plus carrying cost.

q: Under a perpetual inventory system:

options.A: Stock is verified and recorded only at the end of the accounting year
options.B: No stores records are maintained during the year
options.C: Issues are recorded only when the stores are physically counted
options.D: A continuous record of receipts, issues and balances of each item is maintained, supported by continuous stock verification, so that the balance of every item is known at any time

e: Under a perpetual inventory system, receipts and issues are recorded continuously in bin cards and the stores ledger, and rolling physical verification keeps the records reliable at all times.

q: The stores ledger maintained in the cost/accounts office, as distinct from the bin card kept in the stores, records:

options.A: Only the quantities of materials received and issued
options.B: Both quantities and values (rates and amounts) of receipts, issues and balances of materials
options.C: Only the values of materials sold to customers
options.D: The attendance and leave of the stores staff

e: The stores ledger in the accounts office records quantities together with rates and values of receipts, issues and balances, whereas the bin card in the stores shows quantities only.

q: During a year, 60 workers left a factory and 40 workers were recruited in their place. The average number of workers on roll was 1,000. The labour turnover rate under the flux method is:
e: Labour turnover (flux method) = (separations + replacements) / average workers x 100 = (60 + 40) / 1,000 x 100 = 10%.

q: Wages paid for normal idle time — such as time unavoidably lost in setting up machines or in moving between jobs — are treated in cost accounts as:

options.A: Factory overheads, to be absorbed by the production of the period
options.B: Charged direct to the Costing Profit and Loss Account
options.C: Deducted from the wages payable to the workers concerned
options.D: Added to the direct wages of one specific job

e: Normal idle time is inherent in production, like machine set-up and movement between jobs. Its wages are a normal cost spread over output through factory overheads.

q: Under Taylor's differential piece-rate system:

options.A: A minimum time wage is guaranteed to every worker, whatever his output
options.B: A single piece rate is paid for all output, standard or below standard
options.C: Bonus is paid as a percentage of the time saved by the worker
options.D: Two piece rates are used — a lower rate for output below the standard and a higher rate for output at or above the standard — with no guaranteed time wage

e: Taylor's system pays two piece rates - low for below-standard output and high for standard or above - with no guaranteed day wage, sharply rewarding efficient workers and penalising the inefficient.

q: Time booking, as distinct from time keeping, is concerned with:

options.A: Recording the time of arrival and departure of workers for the purpose of wage payment
options.B: Recording the time spent by each worker on each job or process, so that labour cost can be charged to the jobs concerned
options.C: Fixing the standard time allowed for each operation
options.D: Maintaining the leave record of the workers

e: Time booking records how a worker's paid time was actually spent on specific jobs, processes or idle time, enabling labour cost to be charged to cost units; time keeping only records attendance.

q: A machine is used for 2,000 hours in a year. Its standing charges for the year are Rs 20,000 and its running charges are Rs 30,000. The machine hour rate is:

options.A: Rs 10 per hour
options.B: Rs 15 per hour
options.C: Rs 25 per hour
options.D: Rs 30 per hour

e: Machine hour rate = (standing charges + running charges) / machine hours = (20,000 + 30,000) / 2,000 = Rs 25 per hour.

q: When under-absorbed or over-absorbed factory overheads are of a significant amount, they are adjusted to the cost of sales and the value of stocks by means of:

options.A: A supplementary overhead rate
options.B: A revision of the selling price of the products
options.C: An entry in the stores ledger
options.D: A suspense account in the financial books

e: A supplementary rate spreads a significant over- or under-absorption over cost of sales, finished stock and work-in-progress, correcting all affected figures instead of writing the whole amount off to profit.
